title: The Practice of the Three Non’s: No-Thought, No-Mark, No-Abiding
excerpt: The three Non’s — no-thought, no-mark, and no-abiding — are the core practice of the Platform Sūtra. No-thought: with thought, be without thought; no-mark: with marks, be free of marks; no-abiding: before objects, do not ponder. Attain within being unswayed by thought, and without being unbound by objects. No-thought is the great concentration; no-mark is the great precepts; no-abiding is the great wisdom.

inline.s: Excerpted from
The Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch, Finely Explained
No-thought: with thought, be without thought;
No-mark: with marks, be free of marks;
No-abiding: before objects, do not ponder.
One must do the work on the single thought of the present moment;
this is the wondrous method of governing the mind right amid objects.

The three Non’s — no-thought, no-mark, and no-abiding — are the core practice of the Platform Sūtra. No-thought: with thought, be without thought; no-mark: with marks, be free of marks; no-abiding: before objects, do not ponder. Attain within being unswayed by thought, and without being unbound by objects. No-thought is the great concentration; no-mark is the great precepts; no-abiding is the great wisdom.

[The Master instructed the assembly, saying: Good knowing ones! The true teaching in itself has neither sudden nor gradual, but human natures themselves are keen or dull. The deluded cultivate gradually; the awakened accord suddenly. If one recognizes one’s own mind and sees one’s own nature, then there is no difference. It is for this reason that the provisional names of sudden and gradual are established.]
The Sixth Patriarch

instructed the assembly, saying: Good knowing ones! The true teaching in itself has neither sudden nor gradual, while people’s faculties are naturally keen or dull. The deluded enter gradually through cultivation; the awakened accord suddenly. As long as one recognizes one’s own mind and sees one’s own nature, there is no difference between them. For this reason the provisional names of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation are established.
[Provisional name] A false, made-up name. The dharmas have no reality and originally have no name; it is people who provisionally impose names on them. The Lotus Sūtra
in its Skillful Means chapter, the second, says:
“But by means of provisional names one leads sentient beings.”

[Good knowing ones! In this Dharma-gate of mine, from the transmission above, no-thought is first established as the aim, no-mark as the substance, and no-abiding as the root. As for no-mark: amid marks, be free of marks. As for no-thought: amid thought, be without thought. As for no-abiding: it is the original nature of persons; amid the good and bad, beautiful and ugly of the world — even amid foes and kin, and amid words that sting, and disputes — one takes them all as empty, not thinking of requital or revenge; thought after thought, one does not think of the objects before one. If past thought, present thought, and future thought continue thought after thought without break, it is called bondage; but if amid all dharmas one abides thought after thought in nothing, then there is no bondage. This is taking no-abiding as the root.

Good knowing ones! In this sudden-teaching Dharma-gate of mine, from the time of the patriarch Bodhidharma, no-thought is first established as the aim, no-mark as the substance, and no-abiding as the root. As for no-mark: amid marks, be free of marks, not turned by marks. As for no-thought: amid thought, be without thought, not giving rise to mind on thought, not drawn by thought. As for no-abiding: this is the original nature of persons; amid the good and bad, beautiful and ugly of the world, even amid foes and kin, and amid words that sting and disputes, one knows that all these are phantoms (taking them all as empty), not thinking of requital or revenge; thought after thought, one does not ponder the objects of sense before one (before objects, do not ponder). If past thought, present thought, and future thought continue without break, giving rise to thought on thought, it is called bondage; but if amid all dharmas, thought after thought, one does not abide in objects and give rise to mind — without defilement and without attachment — then there is no bondage and one is free. This is taking no-abiding (not pondering objects) as the root.
[No-mark] Not to be attached to marks; amid marks, be free of marks.

[Attachment to marks] To take marks as real, and so love, hate, choose, and reject. [Freedom from marks] To realize that marks are all illusory, and so have no love, hate, choosing, or rejecting. The Diamond Sūtra says:
“Whatever has marks is all illusory. If one sees the marks as not marks
(if one sees the marks as not real)
, then one sees the Tathāgata
(that is, one sees the Buddha of one’s own nature)
(For the annotation, see
The Diamond Sūtra, Finely Explained

[With thought, be without thought] Do not suppress thought so that it does not arise; rather, when thought arises, know it and do not follow it. Suppressing thought so that it does not arise not only tenses the whole body, but once one stops suppressing, deluded thoughts become even more active. [No-abiding
is the original nature of persons

] The original nature of persons is non-abiding; knowing that all dharmas are empty, one therefore does not cling or defile. But the habitual nature of persons is to abide, falsely holding all dharmas to be real, and so clinging and defiling. [Not pondering the objects before one] Not thinking of the objects of sense before one (before objects, do not ponder); seeing is only seeing, hearing is only hearing, the mind vast and without attachment.
The Diamond Sūtra says:
“One should not give rise to mind abiding in forms; one should not give rise to mind abiding in sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas; one should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere.”
The “give rise to the mind that abides nowhere”

is: not affected by the conditions of objects (temptation, hardship, coercion), and practicing the upright mind. Therefore one should do the work on the single thought of the present moment — this is the wondrous method of governing the mind right amid objects.
[Good knowing ones! To be free of all marks without is called no-mark. Being able to be free of marks, the Dharma-body is pure. This is taking no-mark as the substance.]

Good knowing ones! To be free of all marks without, unswayed by them, is called no-mark; being able to be free of marks, the Dharma-body of one’s own nature is pure. This is taking no-mark as the substance.

[Good knowing ones! On all objects, the mind not being defiled — this is called no-thought. On one’s own thoughts, always free of the various objects, not giving rise to mind upon objects. If one merely thinks of nothing at all, and removes all thought so that a single thought is cut off and one dies, to be born elsewhere — this is a great error. Let students of the Way ponder it! If one does not recognize the meaning of the Dharma, to err oneself is one thing, but to go on to urge others, being oneself deluded and not seeing, and slandering the Buddhist scriptures — this is an even greater error. Therefore no-thought is established as the aim.]

Good knowing ones! On all objects and conditions, the mind not being defiled or attached — this is called no-thought. No-thought means: on one’s own thoughts, always free of the various objects (“give rise to the mind that abides nowhere”), not giving rise to mind upon objects (“one should not give rise to mind abiding in forms; one should not give rise to mind abiding in sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas”). If one thinks that no-thought is merely “to think of nothing at all, and remove all thoughts,” this is a great error! For when a thought is cut off one dies, and is born elsewhere, still in the round of rebirth. Students of the Way must deeply ponder this principle! If one does not oneself recognize the true meaning of the Dharma, to err oneself is one thing; but if one goes on to lead others on with this mistaken method, while being oneself deluded and not seeing the Way, and incurring the offense of slandering the Buddhist scriptures — the consequences are extremely grave. Therefore no-thought is established as the aim.

On one’s own thoughts, always free of the various objects, not giving rise to mind upon objects” — this is: “One should not give rise to mind abiding in forms; one should not give rise to mind abiding in sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas; one should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere.” Only free one’s own thoughts from objects; do not let mind arise upon dharmas.
Question: The Sixth Patriarch says:
“If one merely thinks of nothing at all, and removes all thought so that a single thought is cut off and one dies, to be born elsewhere — this is a great error.”
While the Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, says:
“The great Way is vast and empty, cutting off thought and reflection.”
These two statements are contradictory; which should one rely upon?

Answer: The Sixth Patriarch was speaking against the misdirected practice current at the time that took “to think of nothing at all, and remove all thought” as the ultimate. In this sūtra’s later text, his criticism of Chan Master Wolun’s “able to cut off a hundred thoughts” is likewise because Wolun took “able to cut off a hundred thoughts” as the ultimate. Their error lies precisely in taking “removing all thought” and “able to cut off a hundred thoughts” as the ultimate — they are those who know only the great death but not the great life.
Chan Master Dahui says:

“The old man has always loved what Venerable Zhenjing said: nowadays most people attain a body-and-mind quenched into stillness, with before and after cut off, resting and resting, letting go and letting go, a single thought gone for ten thousand years, like the incense burner in an old temple, cold and dreary — and take that as the ultimate. Little do they know that they are veiled by this exquisite state, so that their own right knowledge and view cannot appear, and their spiritual powers and light cannot shine forth.”
(The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue)
In fact, in doing the work of cultivation there are two great stages — guarding (bao) and letting run (ren). On this, the Fourth Patriarch of Chan, Daoxin, has given detailed instruction.
The Fourth Patriarch instructed Farong, saying:

“The hundred and thousand Dharma-gates all return to the inch of the heart; the subtle virtues as many as the sands of the Ganges are all within the source of the mind. All the gates of precepts, gates of meditation, gates of wisdom, and spiritual powers and transformations are all self-sufficient and not apart from your mind. All afflictions and karmic hindrances are originally empty and still. All causes and effects are like a dream and phantoms. There is no three-realm to escape, no bodhi to seek. Beings and non-beings are equal in nature and marks. The great Way is vast and empty, cutting off thought and reflection. Such a Dharma as this you have now attained, with no further lack — how do you differ from the Buddha?

(Note: “Such a Dharma as this you have now attained” means that Farong’s guarding (bao) work — cutting off thought and reflection — is already accomplished; therefore the passage below directs him to do the letting-run (ren) work — letting the mind be free.)

“There is no other Dharma: only let your mind be free, do not make contemplative practices, nor still the mind, nor arouse greed or anger, nor harbor grief or worry. Vast and unobstructed, at liberty in every direction, doing no good, doing no evil, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, whatever your eyes meet and conditions you encounter, it is always the Buddha’s wondrous function. Joyful and without sorrow, this is called being a Buddha.” Farong said: “Since contemplative practices are not permitted, when objects arise, how does the mind deal with them?” The Master said: “Objects and conditions have no good or bad; the good and bad arise from the mind. If the mind does not forcibly name them, from where do the deluded feelings arise? Since the deluded feelings do not arise, the true mind knows everywhere at ease. Only let your mind be free, without further dealing, and this is called the eternal Dharma-body.”
(For the annotation, see
The Fourth Patriarch’s Instruction to Farong
article)
The Diamond Sūtra says:
“One should not give rise to mind abiding in forms; one should not give rise to mind abiding in sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas; one should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere.”

The guarding (bao) work is precisely “one should not give rise to mind abiding in forms; one should not give rise to mind abiding in sounds, scents, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas.” The letting-run (ren) work is precisely “give rise to the mind that abides nowhere.”

[Good knowing ones! Why is no-thought established as the aim? It is only because the deluded, who merely speak of seeing the nature, have thought upon objects, and on that thought straightway give rise to wrong views, from which all the worldly toils and delusions are born. The self-nature originally has not a single dharma that can be obtained; if there is something obtained, and one falsely speaks of fortune and misfortune, this is a worldly wrong view. Therefore in this Dharma-gate, no-thought is established as the aim.]

Good knowing ones! Why is no-thought established as the aim? Because the deluded, who merely speak of seeing the nature, give rise to thought upon objects, and on that thought give rise to wrong views, from which all the worldly toils and delusions are born. And the self-nature originally has not a single dharma that can be obtained; if there is something obtained and one falsely speaks of fortune and misfortune, this is a worldly wrong view. Therefore in this Dharma-gate, no-thought is established as the aim.

All dharmas are phantoms, so the self-nature has nothing that can be obtained amid dharmas; why then give rise to thought upon objects? This is exactly where sentient beings are deluded. One should view everything from the standpoint of the reality of all dharmas — this is the Way.

Worldly people bind their minds to fortune and misfortune, gain and loss; if one can understand that these are all phantoms, with none obtainable, the mind becomes empty, without obstruction, and only then can one enter the Way.

[Good knowing ones! As for the “non,” of what is it non? As for the “thought,” of what is it thought? The “non” is non to the marks of duality and non to the mind of worldly toils; the “thought” is thought of the true-suchness original nature. True-suchness is the substance of thought; thought is the function of true-suchness. It is the self-nature of true-suchness that gives rise to thought; it is not that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue can think. True-suchness has a nature, therefore it gives rise to thought. If true-suchness were absent, the eyes, ears, forms, and sounds would at once be destroyed.]

Good knowing ones! The “non” of no-thought — of what is it non? The “thought” of no-thought — of what is it thought? The “non” of no-thought is non to the marks of duality (right and wrong, good and bad, beautiful and ugly) and non to the mind of the various afflictions; the “thought” of no-thought is thought of the true-suchness original nature. True-suchness is the substance of thought, and thought is the function of true-suchness. It is the self-nature of true-suchness that gives rise to thought; it is not that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue give rise to thought. When the self-nature of true-suchness functions, it can think; if the self-nature of true-suchness does not function, then the eyes cannot see forms and the ears cannot hear sounds.

[Good knowing ones! When the self-nature of true-suchness gives rise to thought, though the six roots have seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they do not defile the myriad objects, and the true nature is constantly free. Therefore the scripture says: able well to distinguish the marks of all dharmas, while unmoved in the ultimate truth.]

Good knowing ones! When the self-nature of true-suchness gives rise to thought, though the six roots (eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind) have seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they do not defile the myriad objects, and the true nature is constantly free (unaffected, undefiled). Therefore the Sūtra Spoken by Vimalakīrti
in its Chapter on the Buddha Land, the first, says:
“Able well to distinguish the marks of all dharmas, while unmoved in the ultimate truth.”
(That is, able clearly to discern all dharmas, while the mind is not moved by these phantoms.)

[Ultimate truth] The supreme principle, that is, the reality of all dharmas. The Buddha says: “All dharmas are false; wherever they cease is called real, is called the reality-mark, is called the Dharma-realm, is called the ultimate wisdom, is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), is called the ultimate emptiness.” (The Nirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll 40, the Kaundinya Chapter)

When the self-nature of true-suchness gives rise to thought, though the six roots have seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, they do not defile the myriad objects, and the true nature is constantly free — this is “give rise to the mind that abides nowhere,” this is “give rise to the mind that abides in nothing.” If one faces objects and then thinks about them and chases them, then there is disorder, there is delusion, there is loss of freedom.
“Able well to distinguish the marks of all dharmas, while unmoved in the ultimate truth.”
— The Complete Awakening Sūtra says:
“For example, the light of the eye clearly discerns the objects before it; its light is complete and full, free of love and hate.”
Master Hanshan says: sentient beings
“have always exclusively taken the arising-and-ceasing mind of delusion to be real; hence amid the six-dust objects and conditions, with all their manifold transformations, they take them for real.”
(The Dream Journey Collection
Reply to Zheng Kunyan, the Vice Censor-in-Chief.) The Śūraṅgama Sūtra
in Scroll the first, the Buddha says:

“You should know that all sentient beings, from the beginningless past, continue in birth and death, all because they do not know the permanent true mind, the pure and radiant essence, and use all manner of delusion; because this thought is not true, there is transmigration.”
